newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU summit seals landmark single currency pact.
newsitem.headline: EU summit seals landmark single currency pact.

text.p: European Union leaders marched forward to the goal of a single currency on Friday, breaking a Franco-German deadlock and sealing a landmark budget discipline pact to bolster the new euro at its launch just two years away.

The leaders also unveiled an initiative to create jobs in western Europe and set their sights on a new EU treaty to be agreed next year to prepare the 15-nation bloc for a wave of new entrants, mainly from the former communist east.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, who hosted the summit in Dublin, said the leaders' ability to crack the thorny issue of a single currency budget pact showed the strong political will in Europe for economic and monetary union (EMU).
But he did not play down the Herculean task the European Union now faced of shaping itself up for the 21st century.
"(Agreeing the new treaty will) need the sort of inspiration which was had by those who framed the original constitution of the United States of America in the 1780s," he said.

Symbolically, on the day the EU leaders sealed the budget pact that paved the way for the introduction of the single currency, European monetary authorities also unveiled their design for the future euro banknotes.

The notes avoid national symbols, landmarks or figures, featuring generic European architectural designs and bridges instead. But they leave space for each member state to put a national symbol if the EU so decides.
The budget pact agreed on Friday was tough enough to satisfy the Bonn government which wants the euro to be as strong as the mark Germans will soon have to do without.
But EU leaders also made concessions to France and other defenders of national sovereignty, by allowing for a political judgement on whether to levy fines on those who overspend.

"This is a victory for Europe. This is a victory for the euro," European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy exulted, saying approval of a "Stability and Growth Pact" had sent the right signal to financial markets.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who had pressed for the strictest possible rules of fiscal orthodoxy, told a news conference he was satisfied with the outcome, even though it fell short of the binding, automatic sanctions Bonn had sought.
"The stability pact is a credible signal that the euro will be a hard currency," he said. Asked whether the euro would be as hard as the deutschemark, Waigel said "Jawohl!" (Yes indeed).

The summit, which on Saturday concentrates mainly on EU expansion, also approved the legal basis of the euro and a mechanism linking it to the currencies of member states that do not immediately join monetary union.
And it formally confirmed Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg as head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) from next July, succeeding Belgian Alexandre Lamfalussy.

Under the compromise budget pact clinched in Dublin, leaders agreed that countries would be exempted from penalties for deficits of more than three percent of gross domestic product if their economies shrank by more than two percent in a year.
But any fine would be subject to a political judgment if there was a recession of more than 0.75 percent of GDP.

The European Commission launched a publicity campaign to ease public acceptance of the new currency earlier this week, unveiling a dollar-style symbol -- a "c" with two horizantal dashes through it -- which is to represent the euro.

While ministers haggled behind the scenes on the final wording of the stability pact, the leaders endured a lecture by British Prime Minister John Major on how they should copy Britain's sweeping labour market deregulation to create jobs.

The growing sense of inevitability about the single currency made this an uncomfortable summit for Major, whose Conservative government, torn over Europe, lost its parliamentary majority on Thursday when the opposition Labour party won a by-election.
Facing a general election by May, Major is under pressure from within his party to rule out Britain joining the euro.

After completing their euro agreement, the leaders moved on to the other main agenda item -- a drive to reform EU institutions in preparation for admitting former communist central European countries from around the year 2000.

The Irish presidency of the EU has produced a report to increase cooperation in foreign, defence, interior and justice affairs but it has left aside for now the issue of greater majority voting, the most sensitive issue to Britain.
